title: Pre-Qualification vs Pre-Approval and Choosing a Lender
description: Learn the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval, why to compare Loan Estimates from multiple lenders, and how agent referrals fit in.
body:
Before you tour homes, it helps to talk with a mortgage lender. The terms can be confusing, though. Pre-qualification and pre-approval sound alike but mean different things, and the lender you pick affects your rate, your fees and how smoothly closing goes.

This post covers the difference between the two, how to compare lenders, and where an agent's referral fits in. I am not a lender, so none of this is lending advice. It is a plain look at how the process works.

## Pre-qualification vs pre-approval

{{img:0}}

A pre-qualification is a quick estimate of what you might be able to borrow. It is based on information you tell a lender, such as income, debts and savings. It is a useful first look, but the lender has not checked any of it.

A pre-approval goes further. The lender reviews your documents and credit before issuing a letter. Because someone has verified your numbers, a pre-approval letter usually carries more weight when you make an offer.

A pre-approval letter is still not a final loan commitment. Final approval depends on the appraisal, underwriting and your finances staying the same until closing. That last part matters. From the time you apply through closing, avoid opening new credit, financing furniture or changing jobs. Any of those can change what a lender is willing to approve.

## Why compare Loan Estimates from more than one lender

After you apply, a lender must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days. It is a standard three-page form, so estimates from different lenders can be compared side by side.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) encourages borrowers to get Loan Estimates from more than one lender, because interest rates and fees can differ from lender to lender. Their [Owning a Home guides](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/) walk through how to read the form.

For context, Freddie Mac reported the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.28% for the week of October 1, 2026, as shown on the FRED rate series. That is a national average. The rate and fees you are offered depend on your own credit, down payment, loan type and the lender.

When you line up the estimates, look at more than the rate:

- The interest rate and the loan type
- Lender fees and other closing costs
- The estimated monthly payment
- Cash needed at closing

Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs, so a difference in fees is worth a close look.

You may worry that several applications will hurt your credit. Credit-scoring models generally treat several mortgage inquiries made within a short period as a single inquiry. Comparing lenders close together is usually less harmful than spreading the applications out. Ask each lender how this works for your situation.

## Know the kinds of lenders

{{img:1}}

Mortgage lenders include banks, credit unions, mortgage brokers and online lenders. A mortgage broker compares offers from several lenders on your behalf. Each type works a little differently, so it is fair to ask any lender how they price loans and what they charge.

Some programs are worth asking about. The [Tennessee Housing Development Agency](https://www.thda.org) offers home loan programs through participating lenders, so ask any lender you are considering whether they take part. If you have military service, the [VA home loans](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/) page explains that program. VA loans typically require no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance, though a funding fee may apply.

Loan type changes the math too. FHA loans allow a down payment as low as 3.5 percent. Private mortgage insurance is typically required on conventional loans when the down payment is under 20 percent. Ask each lender to show you the numbers for the loan types that fit your situation.

## Asking your agent for lender referrals

It is common to ask your agent for lender names, and it is a reasonable question. Your real estate agent can share names of lenders they have seen do good work, but you choose your own lender. You can use any lender you like.

I treat a referral as a starting point, not a recommendation to follow blindly. If I share names, you should still get a Loan Estimate from them and compare it with one or two others, including a bank or credit union you already know. The form makes that comparison simple.

Some questions to ask any lender, whether it came from a referral or your own search:

- How quickly can you issue a pre-approval letter?
- What documents do you need from me?
- Do you take part in THDA programs?
- How do you communicate during the loan process?
- What could change between pre-approval and closing?

## Keep an eye on the market and the paperwork

A pre-approval tells you what a lender may approve. It does not tell you what monthly payment feels right. Try your own numbers with the [mortgage calculator](/mortgage-calculator).

Local conditions are worth a look too. For the four weeks ending September 27, 2026, Redfin reported 5.6 months of supply for the Nashville metro area. Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers. Numbers vary by city, so see the [market data for the I-65 corridor](/market-data) for more.

Two more things to remember once you are under contract. A lender must send the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing. Compare it with your Loan Estimate and ask questions about anything that changed. And wire fraud is real: verify wire instructions by phone using a number you already trust, and never rely on emailed wire instructions.

## Ready to talk it through

If you want help understanding your options or thinking through next steps, I am glad to talk. Fill out the form to [get matched with homes](/buy#form), and I will schedule a call so we are talking within the next 48 hours. You can also [contact me directly](/contact) with questions.

Scott Davis, REALTOR®, Hive Nashville

faq.q: What is the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?
faq.a: A pre-qualification is a quick estimate of what you might be able to borrow, based on information you tell a lender. A pre-approval goes further: the lender reviews your documents and credit before issuing a letter.

faq.q: Is a pre-approval letter a final loan commitment?
faq.a: No. Final approval depends on the appraisal, underwriting and your finances staying the same until closing.

faq.q: Should I get Loan Estimates from more than one lender?
faq.a: The CFPB encourages it, because interest rates and fees can differ from lender to lender. The Loan Estimate is a standard three-page form, so you can compare them side by side.

faq.q: Will shopping for a mortgage hurt my credit?
faq.a: Credit-scoring models generally treat several mortgage inquiries made within a short period as a single inquiry. Ask each lender how this works for your situation.

faq.q: Do I have to use the lender my agent suggests?
faq.a: No. Your agent can share names of lenders they have seen do good work, but you choose your own lender and can use any lender you like.
